html:
Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan general and statesman who led the wars that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Bolivia from Spanish rule. He is known as El Libertador, "the Liberator".

He was born in Caracas in 1783 to a rich criollo family, people of Spanish descent born in America. Orphaned young, he was educated partly in Europe. In Rome in 1805 he swore to free his homeland, inspired by the Enlightenment and by the American and French revolutions.

When Napoleon took Spain in 1808, the colonies began to rule themselves, and the independence wars began. Bolívar's path was hard. Early republics in Venezuela collapsed, and he was driven into exile more than once, finding help in Haiti, the republic born of the Haitian Revolution, on the promise to free slaves. In 1819 he crossed the Andes and won at Boyacá, freeing New Granada. Victories followed at Carabobo in 1821 and Pichincha in 1822. After meeting José de San Martín, who had freed Argentina and Chile, he finished the war in Peru; his general Sucre won the last great battle at Ayacucho in 1824. Upper Peru became Bolivia, named after him.

His dream was a united Spanish America. He led Gran Colombia, joining today's Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Panama, but it split apart amid regional rivalries and charges that he wanted to be a dictator. He died of tuberculosis in 1830, sick and disillusioned. He remains the great hero of the Latin American republics.
